label: Esther — Orit Ge’ez Primary — Complete
summary_plain: Esther tells of the covenant people’s survival in exile under the Persian empire. Mordekhai refuses to bow to Haman. Haman plots to destroy all the Yehudim in every province of the kingdom. Esther, who is queen, risks her life to approach the king without being summoned. She reveals Haman’s plot. The decree is reversed. The Yehudim are given the right to defend themselves. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordekhai. The days of Purim are established as a memorial — days of feasting and gladness, of sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Orit Ge’ez as the primary witness for Esther, supplemented by DSS fragments (4QEsther). The Orit Ge’ez text preserves a longer version that includes explicit prayers to YHWH by Mordekhai and Esther — prayers absent from the Masoretic Hebrew text. The Masoretic Esther is the only book in the Hebrew canon that never mentions the name of YHWH. The Orit Ge’ez corrects this omission: YHWH is named directly in the prayers. The Greek Septuagint additions also include these prayers, confirming that the shorter Masoretic text is a truncation. The Qumran evidence is fragmentary but significant: Esther was the last canonical book to be attested at Qumran, and its absence from certain Qumran collections may reflect sectarian discomfort with Persian-era political theology rather than rejection of the text itself.

key_terms.definition: The Hebrew woman Hadassah, known by her Persian name Esther; becomes queen to King Akhashverosh; risks her life to intercede for the Yehudim condemned by Haman's decree; the book's central figure of covenant courage.

Esther's older cousin and guardian, a Yehudi in Shushan who refuses to bow to Haman; uncovers and reports a plot against the king; persuades Esther to intercede; is ultimately honored while Haman is executed.
The Persian king in Esther's story; identified with Xerxes I (486-465 BCE); holds a 180-day feast, deposes Queen Vashti, crowns Esther; initially unaware of Haman's plot against the Yehudim.

The Agagite official elevated by Akhashverosh; enraged by Mordekhai's refusal to bow; casts lots (purim) to choose the day for the destruction of all Yehudim in the Persian empire; hanged on the very gallows he built for Mordekhai.
Queen before Esther; deposed by Akhashverosh when she refuses to display herself before his guests; her removal opens the way for Esther to become queen. The text does not condemn Vashti explicitly.

Esther 4:14 — Mordekhai's question to Esther: 'And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' — the defining statement of purposeful covenant action at a critical moment.
The festival established in Esther 9:26-28 to commemorate the deliverance of the Yehudim from Haman's decree; named after the lots (purim) that Haman cast to determine the date of destruction.

The Hebrew word pur means a lot or dice used for divination; Haman cast purim to determine the best day to destroy the Yehudim (3:7); the festival of Purim is named from this — YHWH's providence overturned the lot's intended outcome.

The name YHWH does not appear in the Masoretic Text of Esther — a unique feature among Hebrew books; however, the Greek versions (LXX, Alpha-Text) add prayers by Mordekhai and Esther that explicitly name YHWH, and the Greek additions restore the theological framework explicit in those versions.

Two Greek versions of Esther (the Alpha-Text and the Septuagint B-Text) that differ significantly from the MT; both include prayers by Mordekhai and Esther naming YHWH; both were circulating in the Second Temple period and represent distinct transmission streams of the Esther story.

faq.question: Why does the name YHWH not appear in the Masoretic Text of Esther?
faq.answer: The MT of Esther is unique in the Hebrew scriptures: YHWH's name does not appear. Various explanations exist — some suggest it was deliberately written without the Name to allow it to be read in secular settings, or that the Name was replaced in the MT transmission. The Greek versions (Alpha-Text and LXX B-Text) add extended prayers by Mordekhai and Esther that name YHWH explicitly, suggesting that YHWH's presence was always understood to be behind the story, whether named or not.

faq.question: What is the significance of Haman being an Agagite?
faq.answer: Haman is identified as an Agagite (3:1), meaning a descendant of Agag, king of Amalek — the nation that attacked Yisra'el in the wilderness (Shemot 17) and whom Sha'ul was commanded to destroy entirely (1 Shemu'el 15) but did not. Mordekhai is from the tribe of Binyamin (Sha'ul's tribe). The conflict in Esther thus echoes the unfinished ancient conflict — Sha'ul's failure completed at last when Mordekhai (a Benjaminite) defeats Haman (an Agagite).

faq.question: What does 'If I perish, I perish' (Esther 4:16) reveal about Esther's character?
faq.answer: Esther's decision to approach the king unsummoned — an act punishable by death — is a turning point. After Mordekhai's challenge (4:14), she calls a fast among all the Yehudim, then acts: 'I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish.' This is not fatalism but covenant courage: she accepts the risk of her position for the sake of her people. The same YHWH who brought her to the throne for such a time as this will determine the outcome.

faq.question: What is the significance of the lots (purim) that Haman cast?
faq.answer: Haman cast purim (lots) to determine the best day to destroy the Yehudim (3:7). The lot fell on the twelfth month — giving nearly a year before the decree would be executed. This delay, governed by chance, became the window in which Esther could act. The irony is that Haman trusted chance (the lot) to plan the destruction, but the festival of Purim celebrates that YHWH's providence overturned the lot's intended outcome. The name of the festival eternally commemorates the inversion.

faq.question: What does the Greek versions' addition of prayers to Esther tell us?
faq.answer: The Alpha-Text and B-Text (LXX) of Esther include extensive prayers by Mordekhai and Esther that explicitly invoke YHWH, describe the history of the covenant, and frame the story as YHWH's deliverance. These additions were circulating in the Second Temple period and represent a fuller theological version of the story. They show that readers in that period understood the story as a YHWH-deliverance narrative even where the MT left it implicit.

faq.question: What does Esther's story have to do with the covenant tradition?
faq.answer: Esther's story — a Yehudite woman in exile who risks death to save her people — is a covenant story of loyalty and providential deliverance. Even without YHWH's name being spoken (in the MT), the pattern is recognizable: the people are threatened with destruction; a faithful person acts at great personal risk; the enemies of the covenant are overturned; the people are preserved. This is the pattern of Mitzrayim, the wilderness, and the exile — YHWH working through human covenant loyalty.

faq.question: What does the Purim festival celebrate and how is it observed?
faq.answer: Purim celebrates the deliverance of the Yehudim from Haman's decree. Esther 9:22 prescribes: days of feasting and gladness; sending portions of food to one another; and giving gifts to the poor. Esther 9:27-28 establishes these as perpetual days. The book of Esther is read publicly; the community actively responds to Haman's name. The festival is deliberately joyful — a celebration of reversal and survival.

faq.question: What is the relationship between Vashti and Esther in the structure of the story?
faq.answer: Vashti's refusal to display herself (ch.1) and her subsequent deposition create the vacancy that Esther fills. The two women model different responses to power: Vashti refused a demeaning command at personal cost; Esther accepted her position in a foreign court and then risked it to serve her people. The book does not condemn Vashti — her refusal has its own dignity. The two women together represent the complexity of living faithfully under empire.

faq.question: What does Mordekhai's refusal to bow to Haman represent?
faq.answer: Mordekhai's refusal to bow (3:2) is the trigger for the entire conflict. He does not explain his reason in the text, but the narrative framing (his identity as a Yehudi, 3:4) suggests it is a matter of covenant loyalty — refusing to give divine-like honor to a human official. This connects to the broader Hebrew prohibition against bowing to those who claim inappropriate status. His refusal costs nearly everything — but the story vindicates it completely.

faq.question: What is the textual history of Esther and what does it tell us about the canon?
faq.answer: Esther exists in three distinct textual forms: the Hebrew MT, the Greek Alpha-Text (AT), and the Greek B-Text (LXX). These differ significantly in content, tone, and theology. The MT is the base of the later Rabbinic canon; the Greek versions with their theological additions were circulating in the Second Temple period. This demonstrates the fluid text tradition of the Second Temple period — before Rabbinic canonization fixed a single form — consistent with the DSS evidence across other books.
